🐪 Good Wednesday afternoon! Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 584 words, a 2-min. read. Thanks to Sheryl Miller for copy editing.

 
 
1 big thing: What's next for Israel
 
Benjamin Netanyahu addresses supporters at an election night rally. Photo: Jalaa Marey/AFP via Getty Images

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's electoral coalition has opened a sizable lead over Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc with 85% of the vote counted, Axios' Barak Ravid reports from Tel Aviv.

  • Still, neither bloc will clear a 61-seat majority. That sets the stage for weeks of wrangling over the country's next government.

🗳️ Netanyahu will emerge from the election down but not out.

  • His bloc is on pace to secure 53 seats — 11 fewer than he currently commands.

Eisenkot's bloc trails with 48 seats, leaving both men without a clear mandate to lead the government.

  • Eisenkot could theoretically swear in a government with the support of Arab parties — which are on track to secure a record 19 seats — yet that's highly unlikely.
Gadi Eisenkot waves an Israeli flag at an election night rally. Photo: Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images

🤳 President Trump told Axios in a brief interview today that at first he received "horror reports" about Netanyahu's prospects. But, Trump added, "he's in pretty good shape now."

  • Trump said: "I heard my endorsement made a big difference for Bibi."

Asked whether he'll get involved in efforts to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he hadn't thought about it.

  • He said: "I will take a look."

🪖 What's next: There are 500,000 votes left to count, from soldiers, diplomats, prisoners and others who voted outside their designated area.

  • They could slightly shift the blocs' seat totals, or the allotment of seats within each bloc. But they are unlikely to change the overall balance of power.

2. 🎢 Theme park visits slide
 
Data: TEA Global Experience. Table: Alex Fitzpatrick/Axios

Attendance at most of the country's 10 busiest theme parks fell between 2024 and 2025, per closely watched estimates.

  • Traffic at Disney's Magic Kingdom and EPCOT in Florida fell 0.2%, while Universal Studios Hollywood visits fell by 8%, according to the annual TEA Global Experience Index.

🎡 Some theme park fans may have chosen to spend their money and time off last year at the new Universal Epic Universe, which opened in 2025 and drew 4 million visitors.

  • TEA's report also points to a drop in Canadian visitors to the U.S. amid political tensions and a weaker Canadian dollar.

🎸 Stunning stat: Visits to Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., hit 3.4 million, up a whopping 8.1%.

4. 🪩 1 for the road: Another Sphere
 
Rendering: Courtesy of Prince George's County

The Sphere — a 6,000-seat, orb-shaped immersive entertainment venue — got final approval yesterday to be built at Maryland's National Harbor just outside D.C., Axios D.C.'s Cuneyt Dil reports.

  • Local officials are betting that the $1.4 billion mini version of the Las Vegas Sphere will be a big draw.

🏟️ Maryland's Sphere will host immersive concerts and shows with vibrating seats, 4D effects and a 16,000-by-16,000 interior display that the creators say is the "world's highest-resolution LED screen."
